question: How did the campaign grow, and why did it matter?
status: A–F are new factual teaching summaries based on our earlier lessons. No old text, speech, testimony or picture is copied. The model opening is newly written by the lesson author. It is not a quote.

account_fact_cards.title: A setting and reasons for change
account_fact_cards.body: Montgomery bus rules treated Black riders unfairly. These rules had lasted for years. In 1954, the Women’s Political Council asked for fairer bus treatment. Little changed. These grievances gave people reasons to protest.

origin.part: C Unfair bus rules; F Earlier calls for change

account_fact_cards.scope: Background and long-term causes. Existing groups enabled action; their existence is not itself the unfair treatment causing protest.
account_fact_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 2 S1; Week 3 C/F.
basis: Week 3 C Unfair bus rules; F Earlier calls for change

account_fact_cards.title: An arrest helped set off action
account_fact_cards.body: Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus. Police arrested her. Organisers then called for people to stay off buses on 5 December. The arrest was a trigger, not the only cause.
account_fact_cards.scope: Trigger is distinct from long-term grievances and the later boycott start.
account_fact_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 2 context; Week 3 A; Week 4 B.
basis: Week 4 B A refusal and arrest

account_fact_cards.title: Many people sustained the boycott
account_fact_cards.body: The boycott began on 5 December 1955. Many Black residents avoided the buses. They walked or shared rides. Volunteers and local groups raised funds and arranged lifts. Shared effort helped the campaign last.

origin.part: S1 A call to stay off buses; S3 Keeping the protest going
C A protest kept going by many

account_fact_cards.scope: Do not say every participant used a carpool or one leader sustained the campaign alone.
account_fact_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 2 S1/S3; Week 3 E; Week 4 C.
basis: Week 2 S1 A call to stay off buses; S3 Keeping the protest going
Week 3 E New ways to travel
Week 4 C A protest kept going by many

account_fact_cards.title: A separate legal route
account_fact_cards.body: Four Black women continued the case Browder v. Gayle. Parks was not a plaintiff. Federal judges ruled against bus segregation on 5 June. The US Supreme Court upheld the ruling on 13 November. Legal action mattered alongside protest.

origin.part: S4 The court ruling and staff note
P1 A legal case alongside the protest
D A separate case changed bus law

account_fact_cards.scope: Four plaintiffs continued after an original fifth withdrew; no new claimant names required. The boycott did not itself repeal the law.
account_fact_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 2 S4; Week 3 P1; Week 4 D.
basis: Week 2 S4 The court ruling and staff note
Week 3 P1 A legal case alongside the protest
Week 4 D A separate case changed bus law

account_fact_cards.title: The boycott ended and buses changed
account_fact_cards.body: After the court order reached Montgomery, the boycott ended on 20 December. People returned to integrated buses on 21 December 1956. The bus seating rule had changed. This did not end racism or every unfair rule.

origin.part: S5 A call to end the boycott and staff check
B A change to bus seating
D A separate case changed bus law

account_fact_cards.scope: Distinguish announcement/end on20December from return to integrated buses on21December.
account_fact_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 2 S5; Week 3 B; Week 4 D.
basis: Week 2 S5 A call to end the boycott and staff check
Week 3 B A change to bus seating
Week 4 D A separate case changed bus law

account_fact_cards.title: Why the campaign matters
account_fact_cards.body: The campaign showed how shared protest could last. Its networks and example helped later civil rights work. Parks’s part mattered, but so did many residents, organisers and the court case. This was one influence among many, not the end of racism.

origin.part: D Links that lasted; G A model for later protests

account_fact_cards.scope: Significance needs a reason, not just fame or a list of honours. Do not claim this campaign alone caused every later rights change.
account_fact_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 3 D/G; Week 4 C/D.
basis: Week 3 D Links that lasted; G A model for later protests

structured_account.historical_limit: Parks helped prompt the campaign, but many residents and organisers sustained it. Browder v. Gayle was a separate legal case; Parks was not a plaintiff. Changed bus rights did not end racism.

model.text: The bus boycott took place in Montgomery, in Alabama, USA, in 1955–1956. Black riders faced unfair bus seating rules (A). Many local people and groups wanted fairer treatment. This account explains how the campaign grew and why it mattered.
